design_detail: Descriptive analysis of United States commercial insurance claims (MarketScan), published as a three-page Research Brief. All young people aged 15-24 with a medically treated overdose involving a benzodiazepine or a stimulant (amphetamine or methylphenidate) between 1 January 2016 and 31 December 2018, treated in an emergency department or as an inpatient, identified by ICD-10-CM poisoning codes; the first overdose per person, with at least 6 months of insurance enrolment including prescription coverage beforehand. For each person the study counts dispensed prescriptions of the same class in the look-back window, and mental-health diagnoses, and reports the proportions, split by whether the overdose was coded as intentional self-harm or unintentional. There is no comparison group of young people who did not overdose, and no analysis of benzodiazepines taken together with stimulants.
can_establish: How often privately insured young people in the United States who were treated in hospital for an overdose involving a benzodiazepine, or involving a stimulant, had been dispensed a prescription for that same class of drug in the previous month, six months and year, and how that differed between overdoses coded as intentional and unintentional.
cannot_establish: Any risk of overdose from being prescribed a benzodiazepine or a stimulant (there is no comparison group: the authors state they cannot assess comparative overdose liability); whether the drug taken came from that prescription or from elsewhere (for amphetamine the authors say prescription and illicit sources cannot be distinguished); anything about overdoses involving a benzodiazepine together with a stimulant, which the study does not examine; anything about young people without private insurance, or about overdoses that were fatal outside hospital or never treated.

sample.recruitment: Records: the MarketScan commercial claims database, which covers privately insured people in the United States and captures diagnoses and procedures from inpatient and outpatient visits and dispensed prescriptions (p. 1).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Aged 15-24; an overdose involving a stimulant or benzodiazepine treated in an emergency department or inpatient setting, 1 January 2016 to 31 December 2018, identified by ICD-10-CM codes for an unintentional, intentional or undetermined poisoning, initial encounter (benzodiazepine T42.4x1A, T42.4x2A, T42.4x4A; amphetamine T43.621A, T43.622A, T43.624A; methylphenidate T43.631A, T43.632A, T43.634A). First overdose per person only; at least 6 months of enrolment with prescription coverage before it (p. 1; Tables 1 and 2 footnotes, p. 2).
sample.demographics: Benzodiazepine group: median age 20 (interquartile range 17-22), 1556 of 2986 female (52.1%). Stimulant group: median age 19 (17-22), 415 of 971 female (42.7%). Young women were the majority of intentional overdoses in both groups (62.8% and 54.9%) and the minority of unintentional ones (38.5% and 34.2%). Race, ethnicity, region, income and insurance plan type are not reported (Tables 1 and 2, p. 2).
sample.attrition: Not applicable (a single look-back from each overdose). The number of overdose events excluded for insufficient prior enrolment, and the number of people with more than one overdose, are not reported.
sample.selection_effects: Three selections, all named by the authors except the first. (1) Private insurance only: young people on Medicaid or without insurance, among whom overdose is more common, are absent, and so is anyone whose care was not billed to the plan. (2) Hospital-treated overdoses only: the authors state they miss overdoses that did not reach an emergency department or hospital, including fatal overdoses outside those settings. (3) Coded involvement only: events in which benzodiazepine or stimulant involvement was not recorded are missed (p. 3). The requirement of 6 months' prior enrolment also selects people with stable coverage, who are more likely to have had prescriptions dispensed, which would tend to raise the proportions reported.

exposure.measurement: Pharmacy claims for dispensed prescriptions in the 6 months before the overdose (and, in a footnote, 12 months), counted as the number of fills and total days supplied. Benzodiazepines counted: alprazolam, chlordiazepoxide, clobazam, clonazepam, clorazepate, diazepam, estazolam, flurazepam, lorazepam, midazolam, oxazepam, quazepam, temazepam, triazolam. Stimulants counted: amphetamines (amphetamine, dextroamphetamine, lisdexamfetamine, methamphetamine) and methylphenidates (methylphenidate, dexmethylphenidate) (Tables 1 and 2 footnotes, p. 2).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not measured as use. Dispensing is recorded as fills and days supplied, not as doses taken: benzodiazepine group, median 3 fills (IQR 1-5) and 60 days supplied (30-120) among those with a prescription; stimulant group, median 4 fills (2-5) and 120 days supplied (60-180). What was actually taken at the overdose, and in what amount, is not in the data.
exposure.polysubstance: Not addressed, and this is the study's main silence for the question of mixing. Other substances involved in the same overdose are not reported, no overdose involving both a benzodiazepine and a stimulant is identified, and co-prescription of the two classes is not examined; a young person could appear in both tables and the paper would not say so. The discussion notes only in passing that the potential for harm increases with selected combinations of prescription medicines, alcohol and illicit drugs, and especially concurrent benzodiazepine and opioid use, citing two other papers (p. 3).

comparison.controls: None. The only comparisons are between intentional and unintentional overdoses within each drug group. The authors state plainly that without comparator groups they cannot assess comparative overdose liability by prescription characteristics (p. 3).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: No pre-overdose comparison population at all, so nothing can be said about who was at risk: the denominators of young people dispensed benzodiazepines or stimulants who did not overdose are not in the paper.

outcomes.instruments: Counts from claims: ICD-10-CM poisoning codes for the overdose; pharmacy claims for dispensing; ICD-9-CM 290-319 and ICD-10-CM F01-F99 for a mental-health diagnosis in the previous 6 months, excluding the overdose date. Specific diagnoses are in Supplemental Tables 3 and 4, which were not among the files read.
outcomes.validity_norms: Poisoning codes and their intent category are assigned in routine care; where several overdose codes with differing intents were recorded, intentional took precedence over unintentional (Tables 1 and 2, footnote a). No validation of the codes against chart review is cited. Dispensing claims are a reliable record that a prescription was filled, but not that the medicine was taken.
outcomes.operationalization: The measured quantity is the proportion of people with at least one dispensed prescription of the same class within a window ending at the overdose; nothing is measured about the overdose itself beyond its coded drug class and intent.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. Fourteen P values are printed (seven in each table) with no correction, no confidence intervals anywhere, and no statistical test named in the Methods.

analysis.effect_sizes: Proportions only; no effect estimate, no interval, no adjustment. Benzodiazepine overdoses (N=2986): dispensed benzodiazepine in the previous 0-1 month 854 (28.6%), 0-6 months 1243 (41.6%), 0-12 months 1380 (46.2%); intentional against unintentional, 0-1 month 590/1664 (35.5%) against 234/1160 (20.2%), P<.001, and 0-6 months 850 (51.1%) against 348 (30.0%), P<.001. Stimulant overdoses (N=971): 0-1 month 239 (24.6%), 0-6 months 380 (39.1%), 0-12 months 416 (42.8%); intentional against unintentional, 0-1 month 137/388 (35.3%) against 93/524 (17.7%), P<.001, and 0-6 months 219 (56.4%) against 147 (28.1%), P<.001. Among those with a prescription in the previous 6 months: benzodiazepine group, median 3 fills, 60 days supplied, 413 of 1243 (33.2%) with more than 90 days dispensed, 1153 (92.8%) with a mental-health diagnosis; stimulant group, median 4 fills, 120 days supplied, 213 of 380 (56.1%) with more than 90 days, 335 (88.2%) with a mental-health diagnosis. Editors' check: every printed percentage in Tables 1 and 2 reproduces from the printed counts to within 0.06 of a percentage point, and the intent strata sum exactly to each total (1664+1160+162=2986; 388+524+59=971).
analysis.preregistration_detail: A retrospective claims analysis published as a Research Brief; no protocol, registration or ethics statement is mentioned.
analysis.selective_reporting: The anxiety-disorder figure for the benzodiazepine group (73%) and the ADHD figure for the stimulant group (71%) are given in the text but the diagnoses themselves are only in supplements that were not read. No statistical test is named for any of the 14 P values. The class-matched figures (whether the prescription matched the drug in the overdose) appear only in a footnote for stimulants and not at all for benzodiazepines.
analysis.power: Not reported and not relevant to the descriptive proportions; the subgroup comparisons in the stimulant group rest on 219 and 147 people.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Among privately insured young people treated in hospital for an overdose involving a benzodiazepine, about three in ten had filled a benzodiazepine prescription in the previous month and about four in ten in the previous six months; for stimulant overdoses the figures were about one in four and about four in ten. Recent prescriptions were much more common before overdoses coded as intentional self-harm than before unintentional ones (51% against 30% for benzodiazepines over six months; 56% against 28% for stimulants). Most of these young people had a mental-health diagnosis in the previous six months.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The discussion says a considerable fraction of youth with overdoses involving benzodiazepines and stimulants had recent prescriptions, that this underscores the importance of self-injury assessment when prescribing to young people and the need for different prevention efforts for intentional and unintentional overdoses, and that because one-fourth receive prescriptions in the previous month the results suggest an avenue of prevention (p. 3). The gap is modest and mostly in what a reader may add: (1) the figures are the share of people who overdosed who had a prescription, not the share of prescriptions that lead to overdose, and give no risk, which the authors state; (2) the title pairs benzodiazepines and stimulants, and the discussion mentions combinations, but nothing in the paper examines the two taken together, nor any other combination; (3) for amphetamine overdoses the drug may have been illicit, which the authors state and which the class-matched footnote supports (31.8% of amphetamine overdoses had an amphetamine prescription against 64.4% of methylphenidate overdoses); (4) 'recent prescription' means a prescription was filled, not that the medicine was taken or that it was the one swallowed.

timeline.event: Lim and colleagues reported that stimulants and benzodiazepines are the substances most often involved alongside opioids in overdose deaths of adolescents and young adults, 1999-2018, which this paper cites as its starting point (p. 1, reference 3).
This study: 2986 benzodiazepine-involved and 971 stimulant-involved overdoses in privately insured young people, 2016-2018.

replication.where_it_stands: No replication in another population was found among the sources read for this library. The obvious gaps are a Medicaid or all-payer version of the same analysis and a study with a denominator of young people dispensed these medicines; neither was among the files read, so this card does not say that neither exists.

funding.funder: US National Institute on Drug Abuse (Bethesda, Maryland) award 1K01DA050769-01A1; funded by the National Institutes of Health (p. 1).
funding.declared_conflicts: Printed as: Drs Bushnell, Calello, Gerhard and Olfson have no disclosures to report related to this work; Dr Samples has received consulting fees from the American Society of Addiction Medicine (p. 1).
funding.affiliations_note: Authors at Rutgers (Center for Pharmacoepidemiology and Treatment Sciences, School of Public Health, Ernest Mario School of Pharmacy, New Jersey Medical School) and Columbia University Irving Medical Center with the New York State Psychiatric Institute (p. 1). Recorded as context, not as a reason to discount.

what_would_settle_it: A cohort study with the denominator this one lacks: all young people newly dispensed a benzodiazepine or a stimulant in an all-payer database, followed for overdose, comparing periods with and without a dispensed supply and with and without a second class dispensed at the same time, with mental-health history and prior self-harm accounted for; it would turn these shares into a risk and could finally say whether being prescribed both classes together matters.

domains.domain: 1. Sample frame appropriate to the target population
domains.note: A complete frame for privately insured young people in the United States, but not for young people generally: those on Medicaid or uninsured are absent, and the paper's framing (youth overdose in the United States, opening with national death counts) is broader than its frame.
A census of eligible overdose events in the database, not a sample; one event per person, the first.
2986 benzodiazepine-involved and 971 stimulant-involved overdoses; the smallest cell used for a percentage is 147.

domains.domain: 4. Study subjects and setting described in detail
domains.note: Age, sex, mental-health diagnosis and intent only. No race or ethnicity, region, calendar year, plan type, prior overdose, other substances involved, severity, or what happened to the person; the specific diagnoses are in unread supplements.

domains.domain: 5. Data analysis with sufficient coverage of the identified sample
domains.note: Overall columns cover everyone, but the 162 and 59 overdoses of undetermined intent are shown nowhere, and in the prescribed subsets 45 of 1243 and 14 of 380 fall outside both intent columns; the overall figures remain complete.

domains.domain: 6. Valid methods for identifying the condition
domains.note: Dispensing claims are a strong record of a filled prescription (the measured condition), and the ICD-10-CM code lists are printed in full; but no validation against charts is cited, the intent code is a clinician's coding decision with intentional taking precedence in conflicts, and an amphetamine poisoning code cannot distinguish a prescribed medicine from an illicit one, which the authors state.

domains.domain: 7. Condition measured in a standard, reliable way across participants
domains.note: The same code lists and the same look-back windows were applied automatically to every person in one database.

Proportions are appropriate and reproduce exactly, but no statistical test is named anywhere for the 14 printed P values, no confidence interval is given for any proportion, and there is no correction for multiplicity.

domains.domain: 9. Adequate response rate, or low rate managed

risk_of_bias.reasoning: As a count of how often young people who overdosed had recently filled a prescription for the same class of drug, this is clean: a complete census within its database, explicit code lists, and internally exact arithmetic (every percentage in both tables reproduces from the printed counts). What limits it is the frame and the silence of the analysis: privately insured young people only, hospital-treated overdoses only, no comparison group, no test named for the P values and no intervals. It may be cited for: the proportions with a dispensed benzodiazepine or stimulant prescription in the previous month, six months and year among privately insured young people treated for an overdose involving that class in 2016-2018; the difference between intentional and unintentional overdoses; the fills, days supplied and mental-health diagnosis figures in those subsets; and the class-matched footnote for amphetamine against methylphenidate. It may not be cited for: any risk of overdose after a prescription; any statement about benzodiazepines taken with stimulants, with alcohol or with anything else, which this paper does not study; the source of the drug taken; or figures for young people outside private insurance.

key_findings.finding: Among 2986 privately insured young people aged 15-24 treated in hospital for an overdose involving a benzodiazepine (2016-2018), 854 (28.6%) had filled a benzodiazepine prescription in the previous month, 1243 (41.6%) in the previous 6 months and 1380 (46.2%) in the previous 12 months.
key_findings.locator: Table 1, Previous BZD prescription rows and footnote c

key_findings.finding: Among 971 young people with an overdose involving a stimulant (amphetamine or methylphenidate), 239 (24.6%) had filled a stimulant prescription in the previous month, 380 (39.1%) in the previous 6 months and 416 (42.8%) in the previous 12 months.
key_findings.locator: Table 2, Previous stimulant prescription rows and footnote c

key_findings.finding: Recent prescriptions were far more common before overdoses coded as intentional self-harm than before unintentional ones: benzodiazepines, 850 of 1664 (51.1%) against 348 of 1160 (30.0%) in the previous 6 months, P<.001; stimulants, 219 of 388 (56.4%) against 147 of 524 (28.1%), P<.001. The same pattern held at one month (35.5% against 20.2%; 35.3% against 17.7%, both P<.001).
key_findings.note: No statistical test is named for these P values anywhere in the paper.

key_findings.finding: Overdoses involving benzodiazepines were more often coded as intentional self-harm (1664 of 2986, 56%) than those involving stimulants (388 of 971, 40%); 162 and 59 further overdoses were of undetermined intent.
key_findings.locator: Results, 1st paragraph (p. 1); Tables 1 and 2 column headings and footnote a

key_findings.finding: Most had a recent mental-health diagnosis: 2232 of 2986 (74.7%) in the benzodiazepine group and 634 of 971 (65.3%) in the stimulant group had one recorded in the previous 6 months; among those who had also filled a prescription, 1153 of 1243 (92.8%) and 335 of 380 (88.2%).
key_findings.locator: Tables 1 and 2, Mental health diagnosis rows

key_findings.finding: Among those with a prescription in the previous 6 months, benzodiazepines were dispensed as a median of 3 fills (IQR 1-5) and 60 days' supply (30-120), with 413 of 1243 (33.2%) given more than 90 days; stimulants as a median of 4 fills (2-5) and 120 days (60-180), with 213 of 380 (56.1%) given more than 90 days.

Whether the prescription matched the drug in the overdose differed sharply by stimulant type: of 833 overdoses involving amphetamine, 31.8% had an amphetamine prescription in the previous 6 months, against 64.4% of the 146 involving methylphenidate.
key_findings.note: The paper gives no equivalent class-matched figure for benzodiazepines. The two subtype counts sum to 979 against a total of 971 (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: The share with a recent prescription rose steeply in the weeks before the overdose: in the week before, 12.4% of the benzodiazepine group and 8.5% of the stimulant group had filled one, against 0.4% in each group twelve weeks before.
key_findings.locator: Figure 1 (data labels printed on the bars)
key_findings.note: Values read from the printed data labels, not estimated from bar heights. Editors' calculation: the twelve weekly shares sum to 37.0% (benzodiazepine) and 33.9% (stimulant), and the last four weeks to 27.0% and 23.8%, consistent with the 6-month figures of 41.6% and 39.1% and the 1-month figures of 28.6% and 24.6%.

key_findings.finding: Young women were the majority of intentional overdoses and the minority of unintentional ones in both groups: 62.8% against 38.5% of benzodiazepine overdoses and 54.9% against 34.2% of stimulant overdoses were female (both P<.001). Median age at overdose was 20 (IQR 17-22) in the benzodiazepine group and 19 (17-22) in the stimulant group.
key_findings.locator: Tables 1 and 2, Age and Female rows

key_findings.finding: The authors state they cannot distinguish amphetamine overdoses related to prescription amphetamine from those related to an illicit substance, that they miss overdoses not presenting to an emergency department or hospital including fatal overdoses outside those settings, and that without comparator groups they cannot assess comparative overdose liability.

The study examines benzodiazepine prescriptions before benzodiazepine overdoses and stimulant prescriptions before stimulant overdoses separately; no table, figure or sentence reports overdoses involving both classes, prescriptions of both classes to the same person, or any other drug involved in these overdoses.
key_findings.note: Recorded because the paper's title pairs the two classes and its discussion mentions combinations; a claim about mixing benzodiazepines with stimulants cannot rest on this study.

reporting_issues.issue: No statistical test is named anywhere in the paper, yet 14 P values are printed (seven in each table). The Methods state only that results were stratified by intent.
reporting_issues.consequence: Readers cannot know what was tested or how; the P values cannot be reproduced or checked, and there is no correction for the 14 comparisons. Claims should cite the proportions and counts, not the P values.

reporting_issues.issue: No confidence interval is given for any proportion in the paper.
reporting_issues.consequence: Precision has to be derived by a reader. The main figures rest on large denominators, but the subset comparisons (147 and 219 people in the stimulant group) are much less precise than the printed single-decimal percentages suggest.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 2 footnote d gives 833 overdoses involving amphetamine and 146 involving methylphenidate, which sum to 979 against the table's total of 971, eight more. The paper does not say that some overdoses involved both.
reporting_issues.consequence: Most likely eight overdoses involved both stimulant types and are counted twice in the footnote, but this is not stated; the class-matched percentages should be cited with that caveat.

reporting_issues.issue: The row 'Days from overdose to most recent prescription' (median 16 for benzodiazepines, 20 for stimulants) sits under the 'Previous prescription' heading, above the subset block, and the paper does not say which denominator it uses: everyone with a prescription in 6 months, in 12 months, or ever.
reporting_issues.consequence: The median interval cannot be attached to a stated group, so it should be cited only with that ambiguity noted.

reporting_issues.issue: The overdoses of undetermined intent (162 benzodiazepine, 59 stimulant) are counted in the totals but appear in no column, so the intentional and unintentional columns do not add to N, and in the prescribed subsets 45 of 1243 and 14 of 380 are likewise unaccounted for.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor and explained in footnote a, but percentages in the intent columns are not shares of the whole; the two columns cannot be combined to recover the overall figures.

reporting_issues.issue: The two headline figures in the text are rounded in opposite directions from a reader's expectation: 28.6% is reported as 'Twenty-nine percent' and as 'one-fourth' in the discussion, while 24.6% (stimulants) is also 'a quarter'.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the discussion's statement that one-fourth of young people who overdose on these drugs received prescriptions for them in the previous month merges 28.6% and 24.6% into one rounded figure. The table values should be cited.

reporting_issues.issue: The anxiety-disorder figure for the benzodiazepine group (73%) and the ADHD figure for the stimulant group (71%) are stated in the text but their sources are Supplemental Tables 3 and 4, which were not among the files read.
reporting_issues.consequence: These two figures are recorded here as stated in the text; they have not been checked against the supplement, and a claim resting on them should say so or the supplement should be obtained.

verification.source_read: PDF (version of record, Pediatrics 2022;149(4):e2021055226; the file's internal name marks it a proof), pp. 1-4, all pages; Tables 1 and 2 re-read on 300-dpi crops and every printed percentage recomputed from the printed counts, Figure 1 values read from the printed data labels on the rendered page; Supplemental Tables 3 and 4 were not among the files read.
